# NanoClaw Summary

## Architecture

NanoClaw uses a **host-container model** where a single Node process orchestrates per-agent-group containers:

> "messaging apps → host process (router) → inbound.db → container (Bun, Claude Agent SDK) → outbound.db"

Each agent group runs in its own Docker container with filesystem isolation. Sessions communicate via SQLite databases (one inbound, one outbound per session), eliminating IPC complexity. The host routes messages through a user → messaging group → agent group → session entity model, then wakes containers to process via polling.

## Claude Agent SDK Integration

NanoClaw "natively uses Claude Code via Anthropic's official Claude Agent SDK," receiving the latest Claude models and toolset. Users can modify and expand their own NanoClaw fork directly through Claude Code.

## Credential & API Handling

Credentials never enter containers. Instead, "outbound requests route through OneCLI's Agent Vault, which injects credentials at request time" and enforces per-agent policies and rate limits. This provides security without permission-check sprawl.

## Scheduling & Capabilities

The system supports "recurring jobs that run Claude and can message you back," with a 60-second sweep detecting stale sessions and triggering due messages. Additional features include web access, container isolation, and per-agent workspaces with isolated memory and mounts.

## Scaling & Multi-Tenancy

The README emphasizes individual-user focus rather than multi-tenant infrastructure. It's designed for personal deployment on macOS/Linux/WSL2, not enterprise scaling. No discussion of costs, horizontal scaling, or multi-tenant operations appears in the documentation.

# NanoClaw Security Discussion Summary

## Security Issue Addressed

NanoClaw solves **filesystem sandboxing** for AI agents—preventing unrestricted file system access that OpenClaw permits by default. However, critics argue this addresses only one layer of a larger security problem.

## Key Criticisms

**senko** contends: "File system access is not one of OpenClaw's biggest security issues. If that were so, running it in a VM...would solve it." The real dangers emerge when agents connect to actual data and gain action capabilities.

**LelouBil** raises the fundamental concern: "Prompt injection just seems unsolvable" when agents perform useful work.

## Major Security Concerns

**The "Lethal Trifecta"** (per sathish316): access to private data + exposure to untrusted content + external communication ability. Any two or three create compromise vectors through prompt injection.

**Skill supply chain attacks**: AutoPilotAI warns that "ClawdHub had a credential stealer hidden in 1 of 286 skills" that silently exfiltrated credentials—a threat NanoClaw's filesystem sandboxing doesn't address.

## Technical Mitigations Discussed

- **samkim** recommends distinguishing "coding agents" (can write new execution paths) from "product agents" (fixed tool sets), using MCP proxies with permission checks via SpiceDB
- **hardsnow** suggests network sandboxing, domain allowlists, and "surrogate credentials" where agents never handle real API keys

## Broader Context

Multiple commenters note the article appears to be sponsored content from a PR firm, undermining its credibility as objective analysis.

## Running Many Agents Cheaply

NanoClaw is a lightweight, open-source AI agent runtime for developers who want to run Claude-powered automation workflows, scheduled tasks and coding agents without the overhead of a larger platform like OpenClaw. Built by security engineers who'd spent months auditing bloated agent frameworks, it distills AI orchestration to 15 files and ~700 lines of code.

## Container Overhead Management

NanoClaw runs as a Node.js service with Docker container overhead for each active agent. The architecture consists of one host process, one Docker container per session, and a SQLite queue that carries every message in the system.

The lightweight nature of the codebase helps minimize resource consumption. Its codebase is about 500 lines of core TypeScript, contributing to its lightweight and high-performance nature.

## Agent Groups and Scaling

Each agent group has its own CLAUDE.md, its own memory, its own container, and only the mounts you allow. Provider is configurable per agent group.

For multi-agent scenarios, an agent can spawn long-lived companion agents with create_agent — each with its own container, workspace, and persistent memory — and delegate to them over the same message queue. That's enough to build real teams: a worker per task, a manager that tracks what's in flight, a supervisor that pings you for approval.

# NanoClaw Repository Analysis

## What Is This Repo?

NanoClaw is "a lightweight alternative to OpenClaw that runs in containers for security." It's an AI assistant framework enabling agents to operate in isolated Docker containers while connecting to messaging platforms like WhatsApp, Telegram, Slack, and Discord. The system includes memory capabilities, scheduled job execution, and integrates with Anthropic's Claude Agent SDK.

## Author/Maintainer

The repository is maintained by **nanocoai** (the organization/user account). This is the **original NanoClaw project**, not a fork—it's the canonical source at `github.com/nanocoai/nanoclaw`.

## Repository Metrics

- **Stars:** 30.1k
- **Forks:** 12.9k  
- **Open Issues:** 281

## NanoClaw Creator and History

NanoClaw was created by Gavriel Cohen and Lazer Cohen of Qwibit AI agency (Gavriel is ex-Wix, where he spent seven years), and was built on the premise that if you cannot verify what an agent is doing, you should not trust it with your data.

OpenClaw was developed by Austrian vibe coder Peter Steinberger and was first published in November 2025 under the name Warelay. The software was derived from Clawd (now Molty), an AI-based virtual assistant that he had developed, which itself was named after Anthropic's chatbot Claude.

Within two months it was renamed twice: first to "Moltbot" (keeping with a lobster theme) on January 27, 2026, following trademark complaints by Anthropic, and then three days later to "OpenClaw" because Steinberger found that the name Moltbot "never quite rolled off the tongue."

## Fork and Relationship

NanoClaw is **not** a fork of OpenClaw in the traditional sense—it's a separate project created as an alternative. NanoClaw was built by Gavriel Cohen to tackle OpenClaw security issues, with his main objective being to reduce the lines of code to the minimum possible for a personal AI agent.

Based on the search results, I found relevant information about NanoClaw's idle container resource usage issue:

## Idle Container Memory Issue in NanoClaw

Scheduled tasks that send messages via send_message (IPC tool) instead of returning text as result leave the container idle for ~30 minutes until the hard timeout kills it (exit code 137).

### Root Cause

The task-scheduler.ts has a scheduleClose() function that triggers the 10s close timer for task containers, but it is only called when the agent returns text. Tasks that communicate solely through IPC complete with result: null, so scheduleClose() is never called and the container waits for the full IDLE_TIMEOUT (30 min).

### Impact

During this window, all new messages for the group are queued and not processed.

### Expected Resolution

Task containers should close promptly (~10s) after completion regardless of whether the agent returned text via result or sent messages via IPC.

### General Resource Usage Context

For reference on NanoClaw's baseline resource consumption, each Docker container needs ~200MB RAM for the Claude Agent SDK plus skill dependencies (a transformers model adds 500MB+).

# NanoClaw Research Report

## 1. The project is real and verified

**Canonical repo: https://github.com/nanocoai/nanoclaw** — it exists, is public, and is actively developed (~30.1k stars, ~12.9k forks, 1,899 commits, latest release v2.1.17 on June 17, 2026, MIT license). The same repo is also indexed under **https://github.com/qwibitai/nanoclaw** — this is Qwibit AI, the agency of the creators; issues appear under both paths (a GitHub org transfer/rename — both resolve to the same project; fetching the qwibitai URL returned the nanocoai repo).

Tagline: "A lightweight alternative to OpenClaw that runs in containers for security. Connects to WhatsApp, Telegram, Slack, Discord, Gmail and other messaging apps, has memory, scheduled jobs, and runs directly on Anthropic's Agents SDK."

**Lineage (verified, and it differs from the hypothesis in the task):** NanoClaw is **not** a fork of OpenClaw. It was created by **Gavriel Cohen and Lazer Cohen of Qwibit AI** (Gavriel is ex-Wix) and launched **January 31, 2026 — one day after OpenClaw's rebrand** — as a security-first response. OpenClaw itself is Peter Steinberger's project: Warelay → Clawd/Clawdbot (Nov 2025) → Moltbot (Jan 27, 2026, after Anthropic trademark complaints) → OpenClaw (Jan 30, 2026). Sources: [DataCamp comparison](https://www.datacamp.com/blog/nanoclaw-vs-openclaw), [CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/02/02/openclaw-open-source-ai-agent-rise-controversy-clawdbot-moltbot-moltbook.html), [OpenClaw Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OpenClaw), [VirtusLab blog](https://virtuslab.com/blog/ai/nano-claw-your-personal-ai-butler). Official sites: https://nanoclaw.dev/ and https://docs.nanoclaw.dev/ (note: nanoclaws.io appears to be a third-party/squatter site).

## 2. Architecture (from README + docs + The New Stack/Pebblous deep dives)

- **Host-container model:** one Node.js host process routes messages: `messaging apps → host process (router) → inbound.db → container (Bun, Claude Agent SDK) → outbound.db`. Entity model: user → messaging group → agent group → session.
- **Container per agent group:** each group gets its own Linux container (Docker, or Apple Container on macOS), its own CLAUDE.md memory, workspace, and only explicitly allowed mounts. Bash runs inside the container, never on the host.
- **Messaging/queues:** two SQLite files per session (`inbound.db`/`outbound.db`), each with exactly one writer — no IPC daemons or brokers. A 60-second sweep detects stale sessions and due scheduled messages. Channels: WhatsApp, Telegram, Discord, Slack, Teams, iMessage, Matrix, Google Chat, Webex, Linear, GitHub, WeChat, email (Resend).
- **Claude Agent SDK:** runs Claude Code natively via the official SDK inside the container, including self-modification of the user's own fork.
- **Credentials — OneCLI Agent Vault (documented):** credentials never enter containers; outbound requests route through OneCLI's Agent Vault, which injects credentials at request time with per-agent policies and rate limits. Sensitive paths (`.ssh`, `.aws`, `.kube`, etc.) blocked by default (per [Noma analysis](https://noma.security/blog/evolution-of-nanoclaw-and-enterprise-platform-risk/)).
- **Scheduling:** recurring jobs that run Claude and can message back; supports pre-task scripts.
- **Sub-agents:** billed as "the first personal AI assistant to support agent swarms" (Claude Code agent-teams); `create_agent` spawns long-lived companion agents, each with own container/workspace/memory, communicating over the same message queue.

Sources: https://github.com/nanocoai/nanoclaw (README), https://docs.nanoclaw.dev/concepts/groups, [The New Stack](https://thenewstack.io/nanoclaw-containerized-ai-agents/), [Pebblous deep dive](https://blog.pebblous.ai/report/nanoclaw-architecture-deep-dive/en/).

## 3. Known issues / roadmap (verified GitHub issues)

- **Resource cost per agent:** ~200MB RAM per container (Claude Agent SDK + deps; +500MB if a transformers model is added); container spawn time is cited as the scaling bottleneck. [Issue #839](https://github.com/qwibitai/nanoclaw/issues/839): task containers that reply only via IPC `send_message` idle for 30 minutes until hard timeout (exit 137), blocking the group's queue meanwhile.
- **Multi-tenancy / provisioning:** README explicitly positions NanoClaw as single-user/personal, not multi-tenant infra. [Issue #1184](https://github.com/qwibitai/nanoclaw/issues/1184) (open, Priority: Medium): hard dependency on local Docker socket makes restricted K8s (Sealos/EKS/GKE) impossible; proposes a provider-based container interface spinning up ephemeral K8s Pods/Jobs. No maintainer resolution yet. No first-class provisioning API found. [Issue #1067](https://github.com/qwibitai/nanoclaw/issues/1067): Apple Container runtime race on reboot. [Issue #554](https://github.com/nanocoai/nanoclaw/issues/554): no user-exposed cancellation of in-flight agent execution.
- **Idempotency/duplicates:** [Issue #138] scheduled tasks execute twice (race between scheduler loop and queue); [Issue #293](https://github.com/qwibitai/nanoclaw/issues/293) scheduled tasks deadlock behind idle containers; PR #2123 suppresses duplicate text when `send_message` fires. The sibling OpenClaw has an extensive duplicate-reply problem class ([#33592](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/33592), [#34039](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/34039), [#37844](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/37844), [#42681](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/42681) — `deliver()` runs even after duplicate detection).
- **Roadmap direction:** shrink the core further ("a runtime so small an enterprise security team could audit it"); expansion via skills/adapters rather than trunk features ([The New Stack](https://thenewstack.io/nanoclaw-minimalist-ai-agents/)).

## 4. Running MANY agents cheaply — what I found (and didn't)

**I found no official maintainer guidance on shared runtimes, container pooling, or scale-to-zero.** I searched explicitly for "shared runtime / scale to zero / pooling / lighter isolation" — no hits in docs, README, or discussions surfaced. What the community actually does/discusses:

- **Apple Container** as a lighter-weight native runtime on macOS (official README option).
- **Ephemeral per-message containers** — the [nanoclaw-discord variant](https://github.com/jaypyles/nanoclaw-discord) spawns a short-lived container per message, self-destructing with zero persistent state (a de facto scale-to-zero pattern).
- **Channel folding** — docs recommend sharing one agent group across many channels (unified memory, fewer containers) instead of agent-per-channel ([docs.nanoclaw.dev/concepts/groups](https://docs.nanoclaw.dev/concepts/groups)).
- **K8s ephemeral Pods/Jobs** proposal in issue #1184 (open).
- **Managed hosting** exists as third-party services, e.g. NemoClaw at $9/month per agent ([nemoclaw.computer](https://nemoclaw.computer/discord-agent)); [Railway one-click deploy](https://railway.com/deploy/nanoclaw).
- Low-volume baseline: a Raspberry Pi 4 handles 1–2 concurrent sessions ([advenboost guide](https://advenboost.com/nanoclaw/)).

## 5. Security analyses & incidents (this class of personal-agent gateways)

**NanoClaw-specific:**
- [HN: "NanoClaw solves one of OpenClaw's biggest security issues"](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=46976845) — pushback that filesystem sandboxing addresses only one layer: prompt injection remains ("lethal trifecta": private data + untrusted content + external comms); suggestions included MCP proxies with permission checks, network allowlists, and "surrogate credentials" (which OneCLI's inject-at-request-time vault partially implements). Commenters flagged one pro-NanoClaw article as likely sponsored PR.
- [Airia analysis](https://airia.com/nanoclaw-ai-agent-security-risks-shadow-ai/) — shadow-AI/governance risks: local credentials with no centralized revocation, data exfil to external models, no centralized audit trail.
- [Noma Security](https://noma.security/blog/evolution-of-nanoclaw-and-enterprise-platform-risk/) — praises mandatory (vs optional) sandboxing and per-group isolation, but flags indirect prompt injection and agent-generated skills (backdoors/typosquatted deps) as persisting risks.
- [Forbes](https://www.forbes.com/sites/gilpress/2026/03/13/dont-trust-ai-agents-says-nanoclaw-now-fully-integrated-with-docker/) covers the "don't trust agents" positioning.

**Relatives (OpenClaw/Clawdbot/Moltbot lineage) — documented incidents:**
- **Exposed instances:** SecurityScorecard found 135,000+ exposed OpenClaw instances (Feb 2026); a later Censys scan found 63,070 live.
- **Live prompt-injection attack:** Zenity demonstrated a crafted message making an OpenClaw agent silently add an attacker-controlled Telegram channel, enabling remote command/exfil ([The Hacker News](https://thehackernews.com/2026/03/openclaw-ai-agent-flaws-could-enable.html)).
- **Skill supply chain:** Snyk's ToxicSkills study — 36% of ClawHub skills contain prompt injection; 1,467 malicious payloads confirmed ([Snyk](https://snyk.io/blog/toxicskills-malicious-ai-agent-skills-clawhub/)); the "ClawHavoc" campaign planted 1,184+ malicious skills; a ClawdHub skill contained a credential stealer (1 of 286 audited). Exfil targeted plaintext keys in `~/.clawdbot/.env`.
- **Autonomy failures** cited by Airia: an accidental $400,000 disbursement, inbox deletion, malware installed via prompt injection (all OpenClaw, not NanoClaw).

**Honesty notes:** Issue #138's exact URL wasn't directly confirmed (referenced via search summary); star/download figures vary across sources (20k+ per one article vs 30.1k on the repo page — the repo page is more current). I found references to a NanoClaw Discord community existing but no indexed transcripts of its discussions; scaling guidance above comes from docs, GitHub issues, and third-party guides, not Discord.
